L429: Generalized left ample condition and isomorphism of algebras
L430: 
L431: First, we state the dual of the relevant results from Sect. cite41†3 . Every \(\widetilde{\mathcal {R}}_E\)-class of a reduced E-Fountain semigroup S is an incomplete right S-action and a partial function
L432: 
L433: $$ l_{a}:\widetilde{\mathcal {R}}_E(a^{*})\rightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal {R}}_E(a^{+}) $$
L434: 
L435: is defined by
L436: 
L437: $$ l_{a}(b)={\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} ab & (ab)^{+}=a^{+}\\ \text {undefined} & \text {otherwise}. \end{array}\right. } $$
L438: The dual of Proposition cite67†3.3 is:
L439: ### Proposition 5.1
L440: 
L441: Let S be a reduced E-Fountain semigroup. The following conditions are equivalent.
L442: 
L443:   1. 1.
L444: 
L445: The semigroup S satisfies \((((ab)^{+}a)^{*}b)^{+}=((ab)^{+}a)^{*}\) for every \(a,b\in S\).
L446: 
L447:   2. 2.
L448: 
L449: The semigroup S satisfies \((ab)^{+}=a^{+}\implies (a^{*}b)^{+}=a^{*}\) for every \(a,b\in S\).
L450: 
L451:   3. 3.
L452: 
L453: The partial function \(l_{a}:\widetilde{\mathcal {R}}_E(a^{*})\rightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal {R}}_E(a^{+})\) is a partial homomorphism of incomplete right S-actions for every \(a\in S\).
L454: Define a relation \(\trianglelefteq _{r}\) on S by the rule that \(a\trianglelefteq _{r}b\) if and only if \(a=eb\) for some \(e\in E\). If we assume that \(\mathcal {C}(S)\) is a category and the relation \(\trianglelefteq _{r}\) is principally finite we can define a function \(\varphi :\Bbbk S\rightarrow \Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}(S)\) on basis elements by
L455: 
L456: $$ \varphi (a)=\sum _{c\trianglelefteq _{r}a}C(c). $$
L457: 
L458: The dual of Theorem cite60†3.12 is:
L459: ### Theorem 5.2
L460: 
L461: Let S be a reduced E-Fountain semigroup and assume that \(\trianglelefteq _{r}\) is contained in a principally finite partial order. Then, the generalized left ample condition holds if and only if \(\mathcal {C}(S)\) is a category and \(\varphi \) is an isomorphism of \(\Bbbk \)-algebras.
L462: 
L463: Next, we want to prove that \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) satisfies the generalized left ample condition.
L464: ### Lemma 5.3
L465: 
L466: Let \(f,g\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\). If \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\) then \((f^{*}g)^{+}=f^{*}\).
L467: ### Proof
L468: 
L469: First note that \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\) if and only if \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(g)\) intersects every kernel class of f. Now, \(\ker (f)=\ker (f^{*})\) so \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\) implies that g intersects every kernel class of \(f^{*}\) and therefore \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f^{*}g)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f^{*})\). This implies
L470: 
L471: $$ (f^{*}g)^{+}=f^{*}. $$
L472: 
L473: \(\square \)
L474: ### Proposition 5.4
L475: 
L476: The monoid \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) satisfies the generalized left ample condition.
L477: ### Proof
L478: Let \(f,g\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) and assume \((fg)^{+}=f^{+}\). We need to prove \((f^{*}g)^{+}=f^{*}\). The fact that \((fg)^{+}=f^{+}\) implies that \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)\cup \{n\}={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\cup \{n\}\). Since \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)\subseteq {{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\) we have two options. If \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\) then \((f^{*}g)^{+}=f^{*}\) by Lemma cite68†5.3 . The only other option is
L479: $$ {{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(fg)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\backslash \{n\}. $$
L480: 
L481: In this case \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(g)\) intersects all the kernel classes of f except the kernel class of n. Since \(\ker (f)=\ker (f^{*})\), the image \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(g)\) intersects all the kernel classes of \(f^{*}\) except the kernel class of n. Therefore
L482: 
L483: $$ {{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f^{*}g)={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f^{*})\backslash \{n\} $$
L484: which also implies \((f^{*}g)^{+}=f^{*}\) as required. \(\square \)
L485: 
L486: We want to prove that \(\trianglelefteq _{r}\) on \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is contained in a partial order. The following lemma will be useful.
L487: ### Lemma 5.5
L488: 
L489: Let \(f_{Y,X},f_{W,Z}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\). If \(f_{Y,X}\trianglelefteq _{r}f_{W,Z}\) then \(X\subseteq Z\).
L490: ### Proof
L491: 
L492: The assumption that \(f_{Y,X}\trianglelefteq _{r}f_{W,Z}\) implies that
L493: 
L494: $$ f_{Y,X}=ef_{W,Z} $$
L495: 
L496: for some idempotent \(e\in E\). Recall that X is the set of all maximal elements of kernel classes of \(f_{Y,X}\) and note that \(x\ne n\) is a maximal element of a kernel class of \(f\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) if and only if \(f(x)\ne f(x+1)\). If \(f_{W,Z}(x)=f_{W,Z}(x+1)\) then
L497: 
L498: $$ f_{Y,X}(x)=ef_{W,Z}(x)=ef_{W,Z}(x+1)=f_{Y,X}(x+1). $$
L499: Therefore if \(x\ne n\) is a maximal element of a kernel class of \(f_{Y,X}\) then it is a maximal element of a kernel class of \(f_{W,Z}\). With the fact that \(n\in X,Z\) we deduce that \(X\subseteq Z\). \(\square \)
L500: 
L501: Let \(Y=\{y_{1},\ldots ,y_{k}\}\), \(W=\{w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\}\) (arranged in increasing order) be two subsets of [n] of size k. We write \(Y\ge W\) if \(y_{i}\ge w_{i}\) for every i.
L502: ### Lemma 5.6
L503: 
L504: The relation \(\trianglelefteq _{r}\) on \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is contained in a partial order.
L505: ### Proof
L506: Define a relation \(\preceq \) on \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) by \(f_{Y,X}\preceq f_{W,Z}\) if \(X\subsetneqq Z\) or (\(X=Z\) and \(Y\ge W\)). It is easy to verify that \(\preceq \) is indeed a partial order on \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) (it is the lexicographic order on the Cartesian product of \(\subseteq \) and \(\le \)). We prove that \(\trianglelefteq _{r}\) is contained in \(\preceq \).
L507: If \(f_{Y,X},f_{W,Z}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) such that \(f_{Y,X}\trianglelefteq _{r}f_{W,Z}\) then \(X\subseteq Z\) by Lemma cite69†5.5 . If \(X\subsetneqq Z\) then we are done. If \(X=Z\) then \(|Y|=|X|=|Z|=|W|\), say
L508: $$ Z=X=\{x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}\},\quad Y=\{y_{1},\ldots ,y_{k}\},\quad W=\{w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\} $$
L509: 
L510: Since \(f_{Y,X}\trianglelefteq _{r}f_{W,Z}\) then \(f_{Y,X}=ef_{W,X}\) for some idempotent \(e\in E\). Now
L511: 
L512: $$ y_{i}=f_{Y,X}(x_{i})=ef_{W,X}(x_{i})\ge f_{W,X}(x_{i})=w_{i} $$
L513: 
L514: so indeed \(Y\ge W\) and this finishes the proof. \(\square \)
L515: 
L516: According to Theorem cite70†5.2 , Proposition cite71†5.4 and Lemma cite72†5.6 we obtain:
L517: ### Theorem 5.7
L518: 
L519: The graph \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) with composition as defined in Definition cite56†3.7 is a category (with zero morphisms) and for every commutative unital ring \(\Bbbk \) there is an isomorphism of algebras \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\simeq \Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\).
L520: ### Remark 5.8
L521: The fact that \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) and \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) are Morita equivalent (i.e., their module categories are equivalent) follows from the well-known Dold–Kan correspondence [cite73†3 , cite74†13 ].
L522: It is possible to show that \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is Morita equivalent to the algebra of the category of sets \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) for \(1\le k\le n\) and all the order-preserving functions between them — this is the simplex category [cite75†17 , Section VII 5] truncated at n.
L523: According to the Dold–Kan theorem, this algebra is Morita equivalent to the contracted algebra of the skeleton of \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) which is Morita equivalent to \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) itself (see [cite76†36 , Proposition 2.2]). The contracted algebra of the skeleton is the algebra of a straight line quiver with n vertices and the relations are that each composition of successive arrows equals 0.
L524: See also the Lack–Street equivalence [cite77†15 ] and [cite78†34 , Example 4.9].
L525: Associated category

L527: We want to show now that we can give a simple description of the composition in \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\). We start with some useful lemmas.
L528: ### Lemma 5.9
L529: 
L530: Let \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\). If \((f_{W,Z})^{*}=(f_{Y,X})^{+}\) and \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W,X}\).
L531: ### Proof
L532: 
L533: If \((f_{W,Z})^{*}=(f_{Y,X})^{+}\) then \(Z=\widetilde{Y}\) (recall that \(\widetilde{Y}=Y\cup \{n\}\)) but \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) implies \(n\in Y\) so \(\widetilde{Y}=Y\). Therefore \(Z=Y\) and \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W,X}\). \(\square \)
L534: 
L535: For every non-empty \(W\subseteq [n]\) we set \(\max (W)\) to be the maximal element of W and \(W^{\prime }=W\backslash \{\max (W)\}\).
L536: ### Lemma 5.10
L537: 
L538: Let \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\). If \((f_{W,Z})^{*}=(f_{Y,X})^{+}\) and \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W^{\prime },X}\).
L539: ### Proof
L540: 
L541: If \((f_{W,Z})^{*}=(f_{Y,X})^{+}\) then \(Z=\widetilde{Y}\) but \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) implies \(n\notin Y\) so \(f_{W,Z}(n)=\max (W)\) is not in the image of \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}\). Every \(w\in W^{\prime }\) is the image of some \(z\in Z\backslash \{n\}=Y\) and therefore w is in the image of \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}\). It is now clear that \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W^{\prime },X}\). \(\square \)
L542: ### Lemma 5.11
L543: 
L544: Let \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) such that \((f_{W,Z})^{*}=(f_{Y,X})^{+}\). If \(f_{W,Z}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) and \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) or vice versa then \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\).
L545: ### Proof
L546: If \(f_{W,Z}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) and \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(\max (W)=n\) and \(W^{\prime }=W\backslash \{n\}\). By Lemma cite79†5.10 we deduce \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W\backslash \{n\},X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\).
L547: If \(f_{W,Z}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then the image of \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}\) which is contained in the image of \(f_{W,Z}\) does not contain n so \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}.\) \(\square \)
L548: ### Lemma 5.12
L549: 
L550: Let \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\). If \((f_{W,Z})^{*}=(f_{Y,X})^{+}\) and at least one of \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\) is in \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \((f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X})^{+}=(f_{W,Z})^{+}\). If \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \((f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X})^{+}\ne (f_{W,Z})^{+}\).
L551: ### Proof
L552: If \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then Lemma cite80†5.9 implies \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W,X}\) so \((f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X})^{+}=e_{\widetilde{W}}=(f_{W,Z})^{+}\). If \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}=f_{W^{\prime },X}\) by Lemma cite79†5.10 so \((f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X})^{+}=e_{\widetilde{W^{\prime }}}\) where \((f_{W,Z})^{+}=e_{\widetilde{W}}\).
L553: If \(f_{W,Z}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(\max (W)=n\) and \(W^{\prime }=W\backslash \{n\}\) so \(\widetilde{W^{\prime }}=W=\widetilde{W}\) and we obtain \((f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X})^{+}=(f_{W,Z})^{+}\). If \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(\max (W)\ne n\) so \(\max (W)\notin \widetilde{W^{\prime }}\) hence \(\widetilde{W^{\prime }}\ne \widetilde{W}\) and \({(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X})^{+}\ne (f_{W,Z})^{+}}\). \(\square \)
L554: The graph \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) associated with \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) can be described as follows. The objects are in one-to-one correspondence with the set of idempotents \(E=\{e_{X}\}\) (where \(X\subseteq [n]\) such that \(n\in X\)). For every \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) we associate a non-zero morphism \(C(f_{Y,X})\) from \(e_{X}\) to \(e_{\widetilde{Y}}\).
L555: Before we turn to describe the composition we emphasize an important observation. Let \(X,Y\subseteq [n]\) such that \(n\in X,Y\). If \(|Y|=|X|\) then \(C(f_{Y,X})\) is the unique non-zero morphism from \(e_{X}\) to \(e_{Y}\) (note that \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) in this case).
L556: If \(|Y|=|X|+1\) then \(C(f_{Y^{\prime },X})\) is the unique non-zero morphism from \(e_{X}\) to \(e_{Y}\) (note that \(Y^{\prime }=Y\backslash \{n\}\) and \(f_{Y^{\prime },X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) in this case). If \(|Y|\notin \{|X|,|X|+1\}\) then there are no non-zero morphisms from \(e_{X}\) to \(e_{Y}\).
L557: ### Example 5.13
L558: 
L559: The graph \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{3})\) has the four objects \(e_{\{3\}},e_{\{1,3\}},e_{\{2,3\}},e_{\{1,2,3\}}\) and 10 non-zero morphisms. If we naturally draw \(e_{Y}\) above \(e_{X}\) if \(|Y|>|X|\) and ignore the identity and zero morphisms then the graph \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{3})\) is the following graph:
L560: 
L561: cite81†Image: figure a†media.springernature.com L562: Recall that composition in \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) of two non-zero morphisms C(g), C(f) with \(g^{*}=f^{+}\) is defined by:
L563: 
L564: $$ C(g)\cdot C(f)={\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} C(gf) & (gf)^{*}=f^{*},\quad (gf)^{+}=g^{+}\\ 0 & \text {otherwise}. \end{array}\right. } $$
L565: We can simplify this description. Since \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) satisfies the right congruence condition, \(g^{*}=f^{+}\implies (gf)^{*}=f^{*}\) so we can drop the requirement for \((gf)^{*}=f^{*}\). From Lemma cite82†5.12 we deduce that \(g^{*}=f^{+}\) implies \((gf)^{+}=g^{+}\) if at least one of g, f is in \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) and \((gf)^{+}\ne g^{+}\) otherwise. Therefore, we obtain:
L566: ### Lemma 5.14
L567: 
L568: Composition in \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) of two non-zero morphisms C(g), C(f) with \(g^{*}=f^{+}\) can be described by
L569: 
L570: $$ C(g)\cdot C(f)={\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} C(gf) & f\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\text { or }g\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\\ 0 & \text {otherwise}. \end{array}\right. } $$

L572: Maximal semisimple image
L573: We finish this subsection with an observation on the maximal semisimple image of the algebra \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) where \(\Bbbk \) is a field. Let \(D_{n}\) be the subcategory of \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) with the same set of objects but the morphisms are only morphisms of the form \(C(f_{Y,X})\) where \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\).
L574: Note that if \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then \(\widetilde{Y}=Y\) (since \(n\in Y\)) and if \(Z=Y\) then \(C(f_{W,Z})\cdot C(f_{Y,X})=C(f_{W,X})\) where \(f_{W,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\). Therefore, \(D_{n}\) is indeed a subcategory (without zero morphisms) of \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\). Moreover, every morphism \(C(f_{Y,X})\) in \(D_{n}\) has an inverse \(C(f_{X,Y})\) so \(D_{n}\) is a groupoid.
L575: Note also that the identity morphisms \(C(e_{X})\) (for \(X\subseteq [n]\) with \(n\in X\)) are the only endomorphisms in \(D_{n}\).
L576: ### Lemma 5.15
L577: 
L578: Let \(\Bbbk \) be a field. The Jacobson radical of \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) is the subvector space spanned by all the morphisms of the form \(C(f_{Y,X})\) where \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) (or equivalently, \(n\notin Y)\) and
L579: 
L580: $$ \Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})/{{\,\textrm{Rad}\,}}(\Bbbk \mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}))\simeq \Bbbk D_{n}. $$
L581: ### Proof
L582: 
L583: Denote by R the subvector space of \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) spanned by all the morphisms of the form \(C(f_{Y,X})\) where \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\). First note that according to Lemma cite83†5.14 if \(f_{W,Z},f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) then
L584: 
L585: $$ C(f_{W,Z})\cdot C(f_{Y,X})=0. $$
L586: Moreover, if \(f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) and \(f_{W,Z}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) are such that \(C(f_{W,Z})\cdot C(f_{Y,X})\ne 0\) then \(f_{W,Z}f_{Y,X}\notin {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) according to Lemma cite84†5.11 (and the dual holds if \(C(f_{Y,X})\cdot C(f_{W,Z})\ne 0\)). Both facts together imply that R is a nilpotent ideal (of nilpotency degree 2).
L587: Since every non-zero morphism of \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) is either in R or in \(D_{n}\) it is clear that \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})/R\simeq \Bbbk D_{n}\). It is well-known that the algebra \(\Bbbk \mathcal {G}\) of a finite groupoid \(\mathcal {G}\) is semisimple if and only if the order of every endomorphism group is invertible in the field \(\Bbbk \) ([cite26†29 , Theorem 8.15]).
L588: In our case, the endomorphism groups of \(D_{n}\) are trivial so \(\Bbbk D_{n}\) is semisimple for every field \(\Bbbk \). In conclusion, R is a nilpotent ideal such that \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})/R\) is semisimple so \(R={{\,\textrm{Rad}\,}}\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) and the statement follows. \(\square \)
L589: ### Corollary 5.16
L590: 
L591: For any field \(\Bbbk \). The maximal semisimple image of \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is isomorphic to \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\).
L592: ### Proof
L593: 
L594: According to Theorem cite85†5.7 , \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\simeq \Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\). We have just proved that the maximal semisimple image of the last is \(\Bbbk D_{n}\). Finally, it is shown in [cite42†27 , Section 4.2] that \(\Bbbk D_{n}\simeq \Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal{O}\mathcal{F}}\,}}_{n}\) which finishes the proof. \(\square \)
L595: ### 5.2 Binary relations with demonic composition
L596: 
L597: Let \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {B}}\,}}_{n}\) be the set of binary relations on the set \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It is a monoid under the standard “angelic” composition:
L598: 
L599: $$ \beta \cdot \alpha =\{(x,y)\mid \exists z\quad (x,z)\in \alpha ,\quad (z,y)\in \beta \} $$
